questions.q: What is the principal value of cos⁻¹(−1/2)?
questions.explanation: The range of cos⁻¹ is [0, π]. The angle in that range whose cosine is −1/2 is 2π/3.
This is a standard identity: sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 for all x in the domain [−1, 1].

faq.q: What does the miscellaneous exercise on inverse trigonometry cover?
faq.a: It mixes every idea from the chapter: finding principal values, applying properties like sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2, simplifying nested expressions, proving identities and solving equations that contain inverse trigonometric functions.

faq.q: How do I find the principal value of an inverse trigonometric function?
faq.a: First recall the principal-value range of that function — for example [−π/2, π/2] for sin⁻¹ and [0, π] for cos⁻¹. Then choose the angle inside that range whose sine, cosine or tangent matches the given value.

faq.q: Why does sin⁻¹(sin x) sometimes not equal x?
faq.a: sin⁻¹(sin x) equals x only when x already lies in [−π/2, π/2]. Otherwise you replace the angle with an equivalent one inside that range, such as π − x, so the output stays within the principal range.
